name: The Rachel

card.summary: The Rachel is a shoulder-length layered haircut with face-framing layers and outward-flipped ends, used to add volume, movement and a softer frame around the face.
card.note: Cut and highlights need regular trims and salon upkeep.

quick.overview:
The Rachel is a voluminous, layered cut that ends around the collarbone, with choppy face-framing layers that flick outward. It was created by stylist Chris McMillan for Jennifer Aniston on Friends in 1995 and became one of the most requested cuts of the decade.

It appeals because the layers add body and movement and frame the cheekbones and jawline. Updated versions with softer, blunter ends have resurfaced since the 2021 Friends reunion.
quick.how: People ask a stylist for shoulder-length layers with face-framing pieces and often blonde highlights, then blow-dry with a round brush to flip the ends. Descriptions recommend trims about every eight weeks.
quick.risks: The main drawbacks reported are upkeep and styling time. Aniston has said she disliked the cut and found it hard to reproduce without her stylist.

lead: The Rachel is a voluminous, feathered, layered haircut named after Rachel Green, the character Jennifer Aniston played on Friends.[1][2] People choose it for the volume and movement the layers give, and for the way face-framing pieces draw attention to the cheekbones and jaw.

Hairstylist Chris McMillan created it, with colour by Michael Canalé, and it first appeared in the season one episode "The One with the Evil Orthodontist" in April 1995.[1][2] Salons reported surges in requests, and a "Modern Rachel" version spread on social media after Friends: The Reunion in 2021.[1]

chain: Long face-framing layers start near the cheekbones
angle.text: The cut changes the silhouette of the hair: lift at the crown and layers around the face. Descriptions suggest adjusting layer length to face shape, and internal layering for thick hair or layers for the appearance of fullness in fine hair.

paras: The cut is shoulder-length with choppy layers, a side-parted fringe, and outward-flicked ends, usually blown out for volume.[1] Shorter crown layers build height, and longer layers around the face start near the cheekbones.[2] It is often described as a variation of the shag and the bob.[1]
Modern adaptations soften the flip with blunter ends and use balayage rather than chunky highlights, and versions exist for curly hair, bobs and lobs.[2]

McMillan has said the cut grew out of an earlier midlength shag and was meant to blend Aniston's growing-out bangs, with the trend arising from her on-screen presence rather than marketing.[2] It peaked in popularity between 1996 and 1998.[2] Aniston has publicly said she dislikes the cut.[1]

timeline.event: "Modern Rachel" trend after Friends: The Reunion.[1]
